what: Constant-property sensitivity for Lewis Test 35A. Three solver property bases at a matched 20x300 mesh, 20000 iterations, each WITH the 2.5-diameter unheated entry.
controlled: beta was held at 2.23e-4 for all three, so this isolates the effect of VISCOSITY and CONDUCTIVITY alone. None of the three is therefore a self-consistent property set, and none is directly comparable with the earlier runs, which used beta = 1.27e-4. The comparison BETWEEN the three is valid; their absolute agreement with Lewis is not the point and must not be read as one.
nu_reduced_on: inlet-bulk k = 0.5922, matching Lewis, for every basis
finding: Moving the property basis from inlet bulk to mean wall raises Nu by 12-27% over x/d 10-136, and mean film lands between. The spread produced by the property assumption ALONE is of the same size as, and the same sign as, the 19-29% gap between our inlet-bulk case and Lewis's own laminar prediction.
conclusion: The 35A downstream gap is attributable to the constant-property assumption, not to transition. Lewis's code carries polynomial property variation for all properties; water's viscosity falls by a factor of 2.1 from inlet bulk to mean wall.
what_this_does_NOT_license: Selecting mean_wall because it agrees best. That would be tuning the model to the measurement it is about to be tested against -- the exact failure this project exists to detect. The defensible fix is a variable-property solver, which removes the choice, not a better guess at which constant to freeze.
next_step: Re-run with a temperature-dependent transport model (polynomial mu(T), k(T)) and a self-consistent beta, then re-test against Lewis's prediction curve.
